'''Sergey Petrovich Kapitsa''' ({{langx|ru|Сергей Петрович Капица}}; 14 February 1928{{spaced ndash}}14 August 2012) was a Russian physicist and demographer. He was best known as host of the popular and long-running Russian scientific TV show, ''Evident, but Incredible''. His father was the [[Nobel laureate]] Soviet-era physicist [[Pyotr Kapitsa]], and his brother was the geographer and [[Antarctic]] explorer [[Andrey Kapitsa]].

==Life and career==
Kapitsa was born in [[Cambridge]], [[England]],<ref>{{cite web
 |title = Russian Archives Online – Interview transcript – Sergei Kaptisa
 |url = https://www.pbs.org/redfiles/rao/catalogues/trans/trac/trac_kapi_1.html
 |publisher = The Russian–American Center
 |accessdate = 17 March 2011
}}</ref> the son of Anna Alekseevna (Krylova) and [[Pyotr Kapitsa]]. His maternal grandfather was [[Aleksey Krylov|Aleksey Nikolaevich Krylov]], [[List of Russian naval engineers|naval engineer]], applied mathematician and memoirist, and the developer of the [[insubmersibility]] technique. He was [[baptized]] while back in Britain, with [[Ivan Pavlov]] serving as his [[godparent]].<ref name='vandenko'>Andrei Vandenko. [http://www.itogi.ru/obsch-exclus/2008/7/3499.html The witness] interview from the [[Gazprom-Media#Paper publications|Itogy]] magazine №7 / 609, 12 February 2008 (in Russian)</ref> During his late life Kapitsa described himself as a "Russian [[Eastern Orthodox Church|Orthodox]] atheist".<ref name='vandenko' />

In 1935 his family returned to the USSR. Kapitsa graduated from the Moscow Aviation Institute in 1949. He was Senior Research Fellow at the [[Lebedev Physical Institute]], [[Russian Academy of Sciences]] and Professor at the [[Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology]].

Kapitsa's contributions to physics were in the areas of applied electrodynamics and accelerator physics; he is known, in particular, for his work on the [[microtron]], a device for producing electron beams.<ref>{{citation
 |title = The microtron
 |last1 = Kapitza |first1 = S. P.
 |last2 = Melekhin |first2 = V. N.
 |type = translated from the Russian by I. N. Sviatoslavsky; English edition by Ednor M. Rowe
 |publisher = Harwood Academic Publishers
 |year = 1978
}}</ref>  In later years, his research focus was on historical demography, where he developed a number of mathematical models of the [[World-system theory|World System]] population [[hyperbolic growth]] and the global [[demographic transition]].

His activities in science popularization included hosting the Russian Television program, ''Evident, but Incredible'', starting in 1973, for which he was awarded [[UNESCO]]'s [[Kalinga Prize]] for the Popularization of Science in 1979<ref>{{cite web
 |title = Kalinga Prize Laureates
 |url = http://www.unesco.org/new/en/natural-sciences/science-technology/sti-policy/global-focus/science-popularization/science-popularization/kalinga-winners/
 |publisher = United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization
 |accessdate = 17 March 2011
}}</ref> and the USSR State Prize in 1980, and editing the Russian edition of ''[[Scientific American]]'' from 1982 onwards.  He was also active in issues of science and society through his participation in the [[Pugwash conferences]] and the [[Club of Rome]].  In the 1980s he, along with [[Carl Sagan]], was outspoken about the possibility that international [[nuclear war]] would bring about a [[nuclear winter]], making presentations in the US Senate in 1983<ref>{{citation
 |title = U.S., Soviet scientists say nuclear war likely to doom life on earth
 |newspaper = Miami Herald
 |date = December 9, 1983
}}</ref><ref>{{citation
 |title = Limited nuclear war would have profound effects, experts say
 |last = Strout |first = Richard L.
 |newspaper = Christian Science Monitor
 |date = December 14, 1983
}}</ref> and the United Nations in 1985.<ref>{{citation
 |title = Beyond War: Movement takes disarming approach to world tensions
 |newspaper = Los Angeles Times
 |date = September 15, 1985
 |last = Hendrix | first = Kathleen
}}</ref>  He was an advocate of planetary exploration and served on the advisory council of the [[Planetary Society]].<ref>{{cite web
 |title = Advisory Council – Who we are
 |publisher = The Planetary Society
 |url = http://www.planetary.org/about/advisory_council.html
 |accessdate = 17 March 2011
}}</ref>  In 2012, Kapitsa was awarded the first gold medal of the Russian Academy of Sciences for outstanding achievements in the dissemination of scientific knowledge.<ref name="english.ruvr.ru">[http://english.ruvr.ru/2012_08_14/Sergey-Kapitsa-dies-at-84/ Prominent Russian scientist Sergey Kapitsa dies at 84]</ref>

Kapitsa was a pioneer of scuba diving in the Soviet Union, he shot the first underwater film about the [[Sea of Japan]], which was shown at international film festivals, in particular in [[Cannes Film Festival|Cannes]], where it was second only to the film by [[Jacques Cousteau]].<ref name="english.ruvr.ru"/>

Kapitsa was the vice president of the Russian Academy of Natural Sciences and president of the Eurasian Physical Society, and was a strong proponent of restoring support for science in Russia.<ref>{{cite web
 |title = TED<sup>x</sup> Perm
 |url = https://www.ted.com/tedx/events/1128
 |publisher = TED Conferences LLC
 |access-date = 17 March 2011
}}</ref>

In 1992 the [[Committee for Skeptical Inquiry]] (CSICOP) presented Kapitsa with the ''Public Education in Science'' Award.<ref name="Dallas 1992">{{cite journal|title=CSICOP's 1992 Awards|journal=Skeptical Inquirer|date=1993|volume=17|issue=3|page=236}}</ref>

On 14 August 2012, Kapitsa died at the age of 84 in [[Moscow]]. He is remembered for his role in the popularisation of science and, after forty years of hosting ''Evident, but Incredible'', holding the record for being the longest serving host of a TV programme.<ref name="english.ruvr.ru"/>

==Views==
In 2008 Kapitsa signed an open letter in defense of [[Svetlana Bakhmina]].<ref>[https://www.novayagazeta.ru/articles/2008/10/30/36012-v-zaschitu-svetlany-bahminoy In defense of Svetlana Bakhmina] open letter at [[Novaya Gazeta]] № 81, 30 October 2008 (in Russian)</ref>

During the late years Kapitsa was very critical of the state of the popular science and Russian television in general. In one of the last interviews he told about the closing of his TV program: "[[Channel One Russia|Channel One]] ordered me, first, to trash Soviet science, and, second, not to object against [[pseudoscience]]. I refused categorically. Then I was thrown out... They were cynical... The results of their political setups could be felt today: intellectual defeat of Russia, I can't find another word for their activity... [[TEFI]] would've never turned into a one-class dictatorship before. I didn't receive a single TEFI. Only in the past 2008, when [[Vladimir Pozner Jr.|Vladimir Posner]] had left, I was awarded one for "personal contribution to the development of Russian television"."<ref>National Broadcast. Creators and Stars of National Television About Themselves and Their Work. Volume 1 // compiled by Vitaly Tretiakov. – Moscow; Algorythm, pp. 113–121 {{ISBN|978-5926507413}}</ref>{{verify source|date=January 2019}}

Kapitsa was fluent in [[Romanian language|Romanian]] and stated that [[Controversy over ethnic and linguistic identity in Moldova|Moldovans and Romanians are the same people]].<ref>{{Cite web| title=Basarabenii în lume (Colecţie de materiale şi documente prezentate la polipticul cultural-istoric şi ştiinţific omonim)| language=ro | trans-title=Bessarabians in the World (Collection of materials and documents presented at the homonymous cultural-historical and scientific polyptych) | url=http://www.bnrm.md/files/publicatii/basarabenii_in_lume_3.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202010746/http://www.bnrm.md/files/publicatii/basarabenii_in_lume_3.pdf | archive-date=2017-02-02}}</ref>

==Memorialization==
[[File:Сергей Капица на почтовой марке.jpg|thumb|Sergei Kapitsa on a postage stamp in 2015]]
[[5094 Seryozha]] [[Asteroid belt|main-belt]] [[asteroid]], discovered on 20 October 1982, was named in honor of Sergei Kapitsa.<ref>[http://minorplanetcenter.net/db_search/show_object?object_id=5094 5094 Seryozha at IAU Minor Planet Center]</ref>

On 5 March 2014 the President of the Russian Federation signed a decree "On memorialization of {{nowrap|S. P. Kapitsa}}".

On February 12, 2015 the Publishing and Trading Centre Marka issued a commemorative postage stamp and a postmark with image of Sergei Kapitsa.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rusmarka.ru/en/catalog/marka/position/28197.aspx|title=Catalogue|website=rusmarka.ru}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rusmarka.ru/en/catalog/spec/position/28180.aspx|title=Sergei P. Kapitsa (1928–2012), Physicist, Winner of the State Prize. Moscow|website=rusmarka.ru}}</ref>

==Family==
* Father – [[Pyotr Kapitsa]], a leading Soviet physicist and [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] laureate, discoverer of [[superfluidity]]
* Mother – Anna Alekseevna Kapitsa (née Krylova)
* Maternal grandfather – [[Aleksey Krylov|Aleksey Nikolaevich Krylov]], [[List of Russian naval engineers|naval engineer]], applied mathematician and memoirist, developer of [[insubmersibility]] technique
* Younger brother – [[Andrey Kapitsa]], geographer, credited with the discovery and naming of [[Lake Vostok]], the largest [[subglacial lake]] in [[Antarctica]], which lies {{convert|4000|m|ft}} below the continent's [[ice cap]]<ref name=rgs>{{cite news|title=Andrey Kapitsa dies in Moscow |url=http://int.rgo.ru/news/andrey-kapitsa-dies-in-moscow/ |work=[[Russian Geographical Society]] |date=2011-08-03 |accessdate=2011-08-04}}</ref>
* Wife – Tatiana Alimovna Damir (since 1949)<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/sergei-petrovich-kapitza-obituary/|title=Sergei Petrovich Kapitza|first=Larry|last=Greenemeier|website=Scientific American}}</ref>
** Son – [[Fyodor Kapitsa]] ([[:ru:Капица, Фёдор Сергеевич|ru]]) (1950–2017), Russian philologist, folklorist and writer
** Daughter – Maria (1954), psychologist at the [[Moscow State University]]
** Daughter – Varvara (1960), a doctor<ref>[[Dmitry Gordon]]. [http://bulvar.com.ua/gazeta/archive/s19_63859/6147.html Interview] at Gordon's Boulevard № 19 (263), 11 May 2010 (in Russian)</ref>
